message.content:
Here’s a quick rundown of some of the most celebrated (and often sought‑after) sushi spots you’ll find around Tokyo—ranging from Michelin‑starred institutions to more casual but still legendary establishments:

| Restaurant | Location & Atmosphere | Specialty / Highlights | Price Range |
|------------|-----------------------|------------------------|-------------|
| **Sukiyabashi Jiro** *(Michelin 3★)* | Ginza – tiny counter‑style setting (only ~10 seats). | Classic Edomae nigiri served by world‑renowned chef Jiro Ono. | ¥30 000–¥50 000 per person (tasting menu only). |
| **Sushi Saito** *(Michelin 2★)* | Minato Ward – intimate, no‑table service. | Hand‑crafted nigiri using seasonal fish; famed for its precision. | ¥25 000–¥35 000 per person. |
| **Sushisho Masa** *(Michelin 1★)* | Shinjuku – small, cozy counter. | Innovative takes on traditional pieces; known for “Masa’s special” rolls. | ¥15 000–¥20 000 per person. |
| **Umegaoka Sushi Tei** *(Michelin 1★)* | Ota Ward – upscale yet approachable. | Fresh sashimi platters and creative omakase options. | ¥12 000–¥18 000 per person. |
| **Kanda** *(Michelin 3★)* | Chuo Ward – refined tasting menus at a private table. | Seasonal kaiseki style sushi courses curated by Chef Kazuhiro Kanda. | ¥40 000–¥60 000 per person. |
| **Narisawa** *(Michelin 2★)* | Minami-Azabu – modern Japanese cuisine beyond sushi. | Focuses on natural flavors; offers sushi-inspired dishes within broader tasting menus. | ¥28 000–¥45 000 per person. |
| **Ichiran Ramen + Sushi Bar** | Multiple locations – ramen shop vibe with a side sushi bar. | Quick, affordable sushi bites perfect after ramen. | ¥500–¥800 per dish. |
| **Tsukiji Toyosu Market stalls** | Outer market area – various counters across the market. | Street‑food quality sushi straight off the boat; great value if you’re up for crowds. | ¥200–¥600 per piece depending on fish. |

### Tips for Visiting High-End Places
* **Reservations:** For Michelin-starred venues like Sukiyabashi Jiro or Sushi Saito, bookings need to be made months ahead via phone or email.  
* **Dress Code:** Many top-tier restaurants have a smart‑casual dress code; avoid overly bright colors or sportswear.  
* **Tipping Culture:** In Japan it isn’t customary to tip; excellent service is expected as part of the dining experience itself.  

If you’d rather explore somewhere less formal but equally delicious, consider visiting one of Tokyo’s many *sashimi bars* or *handroll specialty shops*, which offer fresh cuts of fish without the high cost of a full tasting menu. Happy eating!
